title: Washington's Black social scene and its audience
summary: The Howard Theatre, Dreamland and Washington's Black upper class and Pullman porters.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: When you were coming up, like you were living in Washington, how did the Negro musicians look at -- how did they see the music scene. I mean, did they feel like they were getting the proper breaks, or did they feel --

Oh, they had their little -- it wasn't that rough, you know, cause there was always some affairs going on, colored affairs, and they had that little circle, they had cabarets down there for colored, had theatre, the Howard Theatre was beautiful, beautiful theatre, real pretty. Club around the corner, called the Dreamland, upstairs. A man named Beckley owned it. I played up there. Played up there. I doubled up there (unintelligible) played with Claude up

there, Claude Hopkins and a fellow named Eddie W____, and all the way (unintelligible) I didn't miss nothing, no kidding and happy,man I was very happy because everything was real fine, real fine, man.
What kind of people came out to hear you all/in Washington.

All kinds, the better class of colored -- we call them the dictiges, that's what, all over, in New York, the doctors' wives, the doctors, and all, Pullman porter was a celebrity because he roamed all over the country with his pockets full. Pullman porter, he was much more than us. (Unintelligible) we was down here and them cats was up there. And they wouldn't fail to let you know it.
